conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been feeling weak and not eating much. I’ve had diarrhea for about two weeks now, and I’ve lost weight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Your primary doctor mentioned your kidney numbers were high and you were dehydrated. You’ve also lost about 10 pounds recently?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I haven’t had much appetite. I feel cold all the time and just tired. I haven’t been urinating much either.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Dehydration can affect your kidneys. We’ve started you on IV fluids to help with that. Your creatinine was high at 3.6, but it’s already coming down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious? My kidneys have always been a little off since the transplant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s an acute issue on top of your chronic kidney disease. We think it’s due to the diarrhea and not drinking enough. With fluids, it’s improving. We’ll keep monitoring it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. What about the diarrhea? It’s been watery and constant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We tested your stool. It’s not C. diff or a common bacterial infection. We’re still waiting on some viral and parasite tests, but no treatment is needed right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had C. diff before. I was worried it came back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s not C. diff this time. Your immune system is suppressed, so we have to be careful, but so far nothing dangerous shows up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve also been feeling shaky and unsteady, like I’m walking drunk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could be from your essential tremor or maybe weakness from not eating. We’ll check your electrolytes and make sure nothing else is going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I take Prograf for my liver. Could that be off?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good point. Your level came back high—12.6, which is above the usual range. That’s likely because of the diarrhea affecting absorption. We’ll lower your dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that help me feel better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It should. High levels can cause tremors and confusion. We’re reducing it to 1 mg twice a day. You’ll need to check the level again tomorrow morning before your dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll do that. What about my liver? I still have hepatitis C.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your viral load is still high, but your liver doctors think we can consider treatment now since your kidney function is improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t take it before because my kidneys were too weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Now that your creatinine is coming down, it might be safe. We’ll discuss it with your liver team after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds good. I’ve been so down lately. I don’t enjoy eating or doing anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. You’re on mirtazapine, which helps with both appetite and mood. We’ll keep that going. Depression is common with chronic illness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ve also been coughing a little, but no fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a chest X-ray. It shows some old scarring in your lung, but no pneumonia. Your heart size is normal too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I traveled for my niece’s funeral recently. I thought maybe I caught something.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of infection now. The cough might just be from dry air or irritation. Keep an eye on it, but I’m not worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are improving. Creatinine is down to 1.5, and your acid levels are normalizing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! Is the diarrhea gone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it resolved yesterday. That’s a big reason your kidneys are recovering. We’ll keep you on fluids today and see how you do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m feeling a bit stronger. Can I eat something light?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, start with small amounts—broth, toast. Your stomach has been through a lot. We’ll advance as tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine culture showed E. coli, but since you have no symptoms of a UTI, we won’t treat it. It’s likely from old infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had UTIs before. Should I be concerned?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. You’re not running a fever or having pain. We’ll watch it, but no antibiotics are needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CMV and other virus tests came back negative. No parasites either. That’s good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing serious is causing the diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not that we can find. It may have just been from a mild virus or your medications. Since it’s resolved, we’ll focus on recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Your labs are stable, and you’re eating and drinking. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What do I need to do after I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: First, check your tacrolimus level tomorrow morning before your dose. Call your liver doctor with the result.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember. And keep drinking fluids?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Stay hydrated, eat small meals, and take your medications as adjusted. Follow up with your liver clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I start hepatitis C treatment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your liver team will decide, but now that your kidneys are better, it’s a real option. They’ll contact you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re glad to see you improving. Take care, and don’t hesitate to call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. The nurse will go over your discharge instructions and medications before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll make sure to read them carefully.
